Sounds like how you have to use _nomap to prevent Google and Mozilla from utilizing your home SSID for location tracking.

It surprises me how many people haven't heard of the WiPS system... So, let's try to get you caught up to speed:

Okay, so, if you have an Android phone and you try to use the GPS (Maps, Earth, etc) while the WiFi is off, it'll prompt you to turn on the WiFi radio for "improved location accuracy." I'm not sure if the iPhone does this, or if it just turns WiFi on automatically without asking the user. The point is that wireless devices use WiFi for GPS... that doesn't seem fishy, now does it?

The reason for this is WiPS. Think of it like a digital world... like the matrix... but instead of digital stores and restaurants, you get a digital map with every single wireless network on earth.

Your home network has a physical location, your neighbor's home network has a physical location, and the same goes for the guy across the street. Now, if you have the unique SSIDs (network names) for all three networks and you know where they are physically located, you can use your device and the strengths of each network being received by that device to triangulate your location without using ANY GPS satellites.

This is beneficial for when you're indoors, or when there's too much tree cover, or you just can't lock onto a GPS satellite. And, obviously, the more networks, the better the location accuracy.

So, a bunch of companies (Google and Mozilla included) came up with this idea and started geomapping private wireless networks around 2009... and they created the WiPS system. They created this digital geomap, kind of like the Matrix but only with wireless networks, and they can compare the WiFi signals your phone receives with what they have documented in order to help locate you, even without GPS.

The problem is that you can't really analyze these networks in real time, so they created a database with all of the SSIDs they could get as well as their geolocation... and you're probably in this database. This way your device just sends the list of networks it "sees," how strong that signal is, and Google's servers do all of the heavy lifting. Then they send you an approximate location based on this information.

But there was a big call for privacy from people who didn't want their information linked to their location and available to the world. So the _nomap policy was created. If you added that postfix to your SSID (linksys would become linksys_nomap) they wouldn't record your geolocation or SSID. Of course, this is only a guideline, and some geocatching companies ignore this completely.

But that's WiPS in a nutshell.
Wasn't there also talk about businesses like retailers using this passive Wifi scanning to track customers as they moved around the store?

Oh, it's WAAYYY more than just talk! They actually use complex algorithms to track where you go, how long you stand in one place (presumably looking at a specific piece of merchandise), and what paths are used the most... amongst a full list of other logged data.

Personally, I turn off my WiFi unless I'm actually using it, especially when I'm travelling. I don't need to use the internet when I'm grocery shopping or picking up new clothes... and, if the rare occurrence that I do need it, I can spare some of my data to check something really quickly.

Let's say that Joe owns a WiFi router and has a password on it. Jane comes over to Joe's house, and he gives her the password to his WiFi. Jane, running Windows 10, decides to 'Share network with my contacts'. Suddenly, all of Jane's friends now have access to Joe's WiFi network, without his permission or knowledge. Now Jane's scumbag friend Steve could go to Joe's house, or park on the street, and access Joe's network. Steve would be able to intercept all of Joe's web traffic, including banking or medical information.

This is a huge security flaw for network owners. This only works if you choose to share the credentials of a network that you own. This is terrible for network owners (including regular people who have WiFi routers) that allow anyone else to access their network.
